summary.text:
An unusually clean annual treasury outturn from a Surrey district that ended 2025/26 with 40 PWLB loans totalling £549,680,000 at a weighted 2.556% — a figure that reconciles to our file to the pound and to the basis point. The paper prints every loan line individually at Appendix C, and once the £37.434m Phoenix Life private loan is netted out of the General Fund row (Table 4 shows it separately as 'General Fund – Other'), the HRA £100m at 3.38% and GF PWLB £449.680m at 2.373% both tie to our position. That is one of the tighter reconciliations we have run this cycle.

The shape of the book is the interesting part. Appendix B shows 82.48% of the fixed-rate borrowing sitting 10 years and over, and only 1.81% — a single £10m HRA loan at 3.01% maturing 28 March 2027 — repricing inside twelve months. Working the paper's percentages against the £549,680k PWLB denominator, only about £20m matures inside two years and about £55m inside five, leaving roughly £454m running beyond 2036 at coupons ranging 1.67% to 3.50%. The paper's own Table at 5.9 prints average PWLB rates of 5.81% (50-year) and 6.06% (25-year) across 2025/26; against that curve, the book is priced roughly 3.5 points below current market. On the DMO's premature-repayment curve at 14 August 2026 all 40 loans sit below par, with an indicative net discount across the book of around £210.7m (38.3% of principal) — the deepest aggregate discount position we have priced this year. Only the DMO can quote and no MRP/accounting treatment is modelled on top.

The balance-sheet identity ties: CFR £679.137m − external borrowing £587.114m − other long-term liabilities not disclosed = £92.023m, which is what Table 3 prints as under-funded CFR. Para 5.5 explains the strategy plainly: the £10m PWLB loan that matured in August 2025 was repaid from cash 'in view of the high-interest rate environment (greater than 5%)' rather than refinanced, extending the under-borrowed position by roughly that amount.

Two things worth flagging internally that aren't for a first-contact email. RBC Investments Ltd, the Council's wholly-owned company, holds £41.9m of loans from the Council at rates 4.22%-7.54% and has now missed two consecutive £309,000 semi-annual interest payments (03 July 2025 and 03 January 2026, £618,000 outstanding). Officers are working through legal/due diligence advice and refinancing options; para 8.3 gives the disclosure but not a resolution date. And Phoenix Life Ltd sits on the book as a 40-year private loan at £37.434m/2.88%/mat 02-May-2061 — an unusual instrument for a district. Both worth carrying forward, neither the right lead for a first email.

officer.subject: 40 PWLB loans, £549,680,000 — and only £10m reprices before 2028
officer.body:
Hi Paul,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts on your Annual Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26, which went to Overview and Scrutiny Select on 2 July and Corporate Management Committee on 9 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your report is one of the more precise outturns we've read, especially the way Appendix C prints every loan line individually rather than the summary tables most councils use, and this is offered in that spirit.

The reconciliation ties to the pound. Your Table 4 shows £100m HRA PWLB and £449,680k General Fund PWLB at 31 March 2026, and our file returns 40 PWLB loans totalling £549,680,000. That's the count, the principal, and the split between HRA and General Fund, all matching exactly. The blended PWLB weighted rate lands at 2.556% on our side and ties to Appendix C once the £37.434m Phoenix Life loan at 2.88% is netted out of the GF row (your Table 4 shows it separately as General Fund – Other). Reconciliations that tight are rarer than they should be.

The shape of what you've locked in is what stood out. Your Appendix B shows 82.48% of the book sitting ten years and above, and only 1.81% — the single £10m HRA loan maturing 28 March 2027 at 3.01% — reprices inside twelve months. The 82.48% at ten years and above works out to roughly £454m running to 2036 and beyond at coupons ranging 1.67% to 3.50%. Given the paper's own note at 5.7 that the 2025/26 curve did not deliver the expected rate reductions, the timing of when that book was assembled has aged well.

The gap between those coupons and where the curve sits today is the corollary. Your paper prints an average 50-year PWLB rate of 5.81% and 25-year of 6.06% across 2025/26 (Table 5.9), against a book weighted at 2.556%. On the DMO's premature-repayment curve at 14 August 2026 all 40 of your loans price below par — indicative net discount across the book is around £210.7m, or 38.3% of principal. That is the deepest aggregate discount position we have priced this year across the councils we have read. Indicative only, of course, and only the DMO can quote — we model no MRP or accounting treatment on top, and whether anything is worth doing with any of it turns on replacement cost and future capital plans this paper doesn't reach. The full curve and every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO discount curve is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity and pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

Three courses fit. Reading the PWLB certainty curve is the natural pair to your Table 5.9 — it covers the standard-to-certainty gap and how the daily curve is set. Understanding the premature repayment curve is worth a look given the shape of your book against today's rates. And Liability Benchmark: the essentials is worth watching given CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates put it in front of everyone. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others in your team or across your Surrey counterparts would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell

officer.voice: Russell Tew, first-person. Deliberately not templated: no bold headers, no bulleted summary, contractions throughout.
